items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha form a connected Hindu framework

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically via realisation of the unity of atman and Brahman, or through bhakti devotion
Karma punishes only in this life
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes toward death.

items.title: Shabbat begins on Friday evening and ends on Saturday night
items.claim: When does the Jewish Sabbath begin and end?

options.text: From sunset on Friday to the appearance of three stars on Saturday night — Jewish days begin at sunset, following Genesis 1's 'and there was evening and there was morning'

items.reveal:
The Genesis creation account marks each day 'there was evening and there was morning'. Jewish days begin at sunset. Shabbat is welcomed with candle lighting (typically 18 minutes before sunset) and Kiddush over wine.

The Torah commands rest from melacha — 39 categories of work derived from activities involved in building the Tabernacle. These include lighting fires, writing, carrying in public, tearing, cooking. Modern applications (electricity, driving, mobile phones) follow rabbinic reasoning by analogy.

Shabbat ends with Havdalah — a brief ceremony with wine, spices and a multi-wick candle marking the separation between holy and ordinary time.
items.why: Religious time is structured differently. Treating Shabbat as 'Saturday' misses both its beginning at sunset and the depth of its observance — one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish practice.

items.title: The Christian Bible's contents were not fixed until centuries after Christ
items.claim: When was the New Testament canon — the 27 books — first listed in its current form?

options.text: By the apostles themselves, before 70 CE
At the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE
Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 CE is the first surviving list of exactly the 27 books; consensus formed gradually through the 4th-5th centuries
By Pope Damasus I at the Council of Trent in 1546

items.reveal:
Athanasius of Alexandria's 39th Festal Letter (367 CE) is the first surviving document listing the 27 NT books we have today. Regional councils (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) confirmed it. The Trent council (1546) made it formal Catholic dogma — partly in response to the Reformation.

Nicaea (325) dealt with the Arian controversy, not the canon — a common confusion popularised by Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code'.

Gospels left out include Thomas, Mary, Peter and the Infancy Gospel of James. Some books that nearly made it (the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement) didn't.
items.why: The 'received text' image of Scripture obscures a long, contested human process. Knowing the canon was assembled doesn't disprove faith — but it changes the questions you can ask.
